author: Robert Riesen
title: Amazon's ( AMZN ) enterprise value now stands at more than
text:
Amazon's ( AMZN ) enterprise value now stands at more than $700 billion, which means it's now ahead of Microsoft ( MSFT ) and only trailing Apple ( AAPL ). There are many reasons I like both Microsoft and Apple, but Amazon just doesn't live up to the hype when you dig into the numbers. In my opinion, Amazon is richly valued on one basic theory. It's the idea that building out a massive distribution network will one day lower costs, increase profits, and yield superior margins relative to other retailers. In economics, this is known as economies of scale. This makes sense in theory, but has yet to come to fruition for Amazon. There are many reasons I won't buy Amazon's stock, but the focus of this article will be on Amazon's cost structure, its true gross margins, and how those margins are presented.
Operating Expense is Increasing Faster Than Revenue Last year, Amazon grew sales by a whopping 31% to $178 billion . That's impressive until you see that operating expense also grew by 32%. This is a big red flag to me and has kept Amazon from improving profits and free cash flow. Bulls contest that Amazon is investing all of its profits into growth, but I think that's mostly incorrect. Most of what Amazon recognizes in operating expense (per GAAP) is what was spent to produce that revenue. Investments into software, data centers, and fulfillment centers get logged into fixed assets and get depreciated over a long period of time. A much more logical assessment is that Amazon's costs to run its business are increasing and economies of scale haven't yet materialized. No company spends money they don't have to, so I assume that Amazon needs to keep spending substantial amounts of money to sustain its growth. One of the main culprits here is out-of-control fulfillment costs, which I'll discuss more below.
